title: Knowing you don't know
hookLine: to know that you don't know is best (Tao Te Ching 71)

cards: A meeting. Someone asks a question across the table, and every head turns your way. You half know the answer.

Maybe a third. There's a small, fast pressure to fill the silence with something that sounds right. Three short words would end it honestly, and in a room full of waiting faces, they can be hard to say.
Chapter seventy-one of the Tao Te Ching is short, and it's built around those words.

teach.b: First, the line itself. To know that you don't know is highest. Not to know, and to think you know, is a sickness.
Two kinds of not knowing: one is aware of itself, the other is wearing a costume. Second, the turn. The chapter keeps playing with that word sickness.
Only when you treat the sickness as a sickness, it says, are you free of it. The sage isn't sick, because the sage sees the sickness for what it is.
Nobody is immune to pretending to know; the sage's health is just catching it. Third, a neighbor.

In Plato's Apology, Socrates tells the jury he went around questioning people with a reputation for wisdom, and came away thinking he had one small edge on them: they thought they knew what they didn't, and he didn't think he knew.
Two thinkers, far apart, arriving at the same door; neither is borrowing from the other.
Fourth, where a real conversation starts.
I don't know isn't the end of a conversation. It's where a real one begins. It lets the other person teach you, and it keeps a guess from hardening into a fact that others then build on.
It's also a relief: you put down the work of seeming. Chapter seventy-one doesn't praise ignorance. It praises knowing where your knowing stops.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-one as a check on false confidence: being aware of the limits of what you know is counted the healthiest kind of knowing.

games.q: what does “knowing you don't know” mean?
o: being aware of where your own knowledge stops
pretending to be unsure so others will feel smart
a secret teaching that only the sage can know

p: thinking you know when you don't

s: chapter seventy-one praises not knowing anything
it praises knowing that you don't know: seeing where your knowing stops.
the chapter says the sage is free of the sickness by seeing it as a sickness
the sage isn't immune; the sage recognizes it.
in Plato's Apology, Socrates says his edge was not thinking he knew what he didn't
the people he questioned thought they knew; he didn't think so.

games.q: every head at the table turns to you. you half know the answer. what does chapter seventy-one count highest?
o: answer confidently and fix it later.
know that you don't know, and say so.
games.why: to know that you don't know is highest. thinking you know when you don't is what the chapter calls a sickness.

practice: Bring to mind something you've been acting as if you understand: a topic, a person, a decision, maybe something about yourself.
Silently, say to it: I don't know, and notice what happens in the body; some tightness may let go, some may grip harder. Stay with the open space those words leave.

wordCard.voice: Knowing you don't know. Chapter seventy-one: to know that you don't know is highest; to think you know when you don't is a sickness. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: to know not-knowing, the opening of chapter seventy-one.

carryVoice: Your line: I don't know. Three honest words. Back tomorrow, same hill.
